exactRecord.title: Choose a cross-sectional study after a limited focal examination

cues.phrase: Ultrasound does not trace the appendix because of overlying bowel
cues.why: The failed modality is explicitly identified, making repetition of the same focused examination an obvious foil.

cues.phrase: a small simple ovarian cyst, but no lesion corresponding to the maximal tenderness
cues.why: This supplies a benign interpretation and site mismatch that specifically neutralize the pelvic-ultrasound option.

fairness: CT is a defensible next modality in this nonpregnant adult with ongoing concern. If the task is a literal imaging request, contrast/protocol details are not specified; the current answer can only be judged at modality level.
Importance: high. Realism: ultrasound can precede CT, but persistent focal pain and rising inflammatory markers require a clearly acute assessment pathway rather than a leisurely clinic return.
The migratory pain plus a nondiagnostic ultrasound is too familiar for a moderate PGY-2/3 item.
suggestions: Compare three credible imaging requests or protocols for a supported clinical constraint, rather than CT against a visibly unsuccessful scan and a dismissed ovarian finding.
Retain pregnancy and stability information where needed; do not add invented contrast contraindications.
Clarify urgency and whether the learner chooses modality or the complete request.

exactRecord.title: Choose the CT request when urinary findings compete with an acute abdomen
fairness: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT is a defensible best offered request for this inflammatory acute-abdominal presentation. Haematuria creates a plausible renal-colic temptation, but delayed CT urography is a weak acute-care competitor.

Too easy for PGY-2/3: classic migratory pain, focal guarding and rising inflammatory markers make the intended protocol routine. Recognizing appendicitis and recalling its usual CT request is not a substantial second inference.

Importance: high. Realism: the hospital setting, pregnancy assessment and contrast-related observations are coherent. These safety facts are not independently exploitable wording cues and should not be removed simply to make the item harder.
suggestions: Keep the concrete CT-protocol task, but use a supported case where the urinary/inflammatory interpretation or a genuine acquisition constraint changes the protocol choice.
Replace excretory-phase urography with a credible same-stage request. Do not introduce unsupported contrast contraindications or numeric thresholds.

assignment.ownerDirection: I feel like they are still a little confusing and we may be missing some of the concepts that are most tested and testable. ... look up everything they can about that topic and decide what concepts on that are the most testable. Then look at all the questions that fit in that topic category and critically analyze if it is a good question based on the rules and feedback you have gotten from me on what is a good and what is a bad question. Then the worker also looks for gaps on that topic that it can fill in with more questions. Remember to try to create multiple part questions when possible. ... The goal of this is to increase the number of questions, fill gaps, test the testable stuff, and to make the current existing questions better and more accurate. Also remember that the questions need to be difficult.

The acquisition covered the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast. During hospital observation, tenderness became more focal on the right and involuntary guarding developed. Pregnancy testing is negative and her circulation remains stable.

decisionNodes.stem: Which hospital evaluation should be recommended now for {patientName}'s worsening right-sided abdominal findings?

answerChoices.label: Repeat contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: A repeat scan can help when the original acquisition was inadequate or a new localization problem develops. Here, adequate imaging has been followed by a progressively abnormal serial examination, supporting exploration.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to diagnostic abdominal laparoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive focal pain with new involuntary guarding keeps an operative abdominal cause consequential despite the adequate negative CT. Exploration can establish and treat the cause.

answerChoices.label: Continue serial abdominal examinations in hospital
answerChoices.rationale: Observation was a reasonable response to the initial negative scan. The newly progressive focal findings change the balance toward exploration.

decisionNodes.explanation: The CT was adequate, so its negative result initially supported observation. The subsequent focal progression and involuntary guarding require a fresh decision. WSES guidance supports exploration for persistent or progressive pain after negative imaging.
sourceLabels: Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis, 2020 WSES update
ASCRS clinical practice guidelines for appendiceal neoplasms, 2025
NIDDK treatment for appendicitis

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At clinic follow-up, {patientName}'s hospital record documents an intact appendectomy. The outside review examined one tip block containing low-grade mucinous lining. Expert permanent review of the entire specimen maps a separate proximal focus of irregular malignant glands infiltrating mesoappendiceal fat. The base margin is clear. Chest, abdominal and pelvic staging shows no distant lesions or deposits on serosal surfaces. Colonoscopy shows no separate colonic lesion. She has recovered and is fit for surgery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s appendiceal tumor after the complete specimen review?

answerChoices.label: Surveillance after the appendectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The tip block does not represent the whole lesion. The separately mapped infiltrative focus changes the tumor classification and creates a regional nodal indication despite local margin clearance.

answerChoices.label: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The complete specimen establishes invasive glandular disease beyond the nonrepresentative tip block. With no represented distant or serosal disease, regional resection and nodal assessment are appropriate even though the appendectomy margin is clear.

answerChoices.label: Cytoreduction with intraperitoneal chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Mesoappendiceal invasion is not the same finding as tumor deposits distributed on peritoneal surfaces. The current complete-specimen and staging record supports the regional pathway; cytoreduction and intraperitoneal treatment require a different disease distribution and specialist assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: A benign-appearing or low-grade sampled region cannot classify unsampled parts of a heterogeneous appendix. The full specimen demonstrates infiltrative glandular disease. A clear base addresses the local margin; it does not address regional nodes. Mesoappendiceal invasion without demonstrated serosal dissemination supports right hemicolectomy rather than the peritoneal-disease pathway.

manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without the separate invasive focus, the whole-lesion conclusion and regional recommendation are unsupported. item.title: Invasive appendiceal adenocarcinoma after complete specimen review
fairness: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes is the single best offered plan: the full specimen demonstrates infiltrative malignant glands extending into mesoappendiceal fat, staging does not demonstrate peritoneal or distant disease, and the patient is fit. A clear appendiceal base does not settle regional nodal management.

The two consequential steps are recognizing that a limited low-grade tip sample does not characterize the separate invasive proximal focus, then distinguishing regional oncologic resection from either surveillance or a peritoneal-treatment pathway. These are standard, testable appendiceal-neoplasm distinctions.

The words 'Expert permanent review of the entire specimen' establish sampling scope; they do not uniquely match an option. 'No distant lesions or deposits on serosal surfaces' is necessary staging information, not an unfair diagnosis giveaway. Options have comparable operative specificity and no convergence or absolute-wording shortcut was identified.

The follow-up coherently supplies the intervening appendectomy, complete pathology, staging and recovery. It stands alone with its presentation and update. The preceding exploration explanation does not teach the tumor operation.

This is an offline editorial judgment from the supplied candidate text, not fresh guideline verification or clinical approval. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified; Melissa's exact-version clinical review remains necessary. The same verification limitation applies throughout this report.
suggestions: Retain the complete-specimen versus tip-sample distinction, clear-margin finding and staging information; removing those would weaken the intended competing decisions.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy with targeted mucosal sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The images and specimen labels from the earlier luminal study do not represent the cecum. Complete luminal evaluation can identify and sample a cecal primary and assess synchronous colonic lesions before planning an appendiceal or colonic resection. It cannot dismiss an extramural appendiceal lesion when mucosa is normal.

answerChoices.label: Repeat contrast CT after inflammatory resolution
answerChoices.rationale: Later CT can define the appendiceal base and extraluminal origin more clearly as inflammation subsides. It does not substitute for examination and sampling of a possible cecal mucosal lesion or the unexamined proximal colon.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core sampling of the junctional mass
answerChoices.rationale: A core from the extra-luminal junctional target would not provide a complete colonic mucosal examination. The origin is still uncertain and the current unexamined cecal compartment matters for the planned operation. The guideline supports colonoscopy for suspected appendiceal neoplasia; this is not a universal prohibition on image-guided biopsy.

after.explanation: The previous report covers the visualized colon, not the cecum: its images and biopsy labels stop distally. A persistent appendiceal-cecal junction lesion therefore still requires complete colonic mucosal assessment, including the possibility of a cecal primary and synchronous lesions. Normal mucosa would not exclude an appendiceal mural lesion. Later CT after inflammatory resolution still has a separate role in localizing the appendix and its base.

item.title: Persistent appendiceal lesion despite normal colonoscopy
fairness: The resident must interpret normal luminal findings as insufficient to dismiss a persistent appendiceal mural lesion, then choose limited intact excision rather than surveillance or an unproven oncologic extension. Both distinctions affect the proposed care.
The later CT adds consequential localization and base-clearance information that the initial presentation lacked. This supports the extent decision rather than simply repeating an earlier conclusion.

The record supports interval appendectomy as the best offered plan in this fit older patient with persistent suspicious imaging. This is not a blanket recommendation for every patient after an abscess; the explanation appropriately limits the application.

The sequence is coherent, and the update independently supplies the colonoscopy and repeat-imaging results. Earlier feedback establishes a neoplasm workup but does not name the keyed operation. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for cytoreduction and intraperitoneal therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Low-grade mucinous epithelium in the separately labelled diaphragmatic nodule demonstrates cellular disease outside the appendix. answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for follow-up without resection
answerChoices.rationale: Margin-negative noninfiltrative disease confined to an intact appendix could support this pathway. The separate diaphragmatic nodule contains mucinous epithelium, so the appendix margin and negative pelvic nodule cannot establish confinement.

answerChoices.label: Multidisciplinary review for right hemicolectomy and nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The whole appendix does not show destructive glandular invasion requiring the localized adenocarcinoma nodal pathway. The demonstrated tumor is in a separate surface deposit; a regional colectomy does not by itself address that distribution.

after.explanation: The specimens represent different sites. A negative pelvic nodule and a clear appendiceal margin do not negate low-grade mucinous epithelium in the diaphragmatic nodule. That finding changes the disease field beyond the appendix. Experienced-center assessment for cytoreduction and possible intraperitoneal therapy is appropriate; this is not a promise of HIPEC or evidence that every deposit has been sampled. Regional colectomy is not a substitute for evaluating the demonstrated surface disease.

after.currentUpdate: Dedicated liver MRI obtained after the staging CT resolves both previously indeterminate lesions. Each has uniform low T1 and high T2 signal, a smooth thin wall, and no mural nodule or enhancement on the acquired precontrast and postcontrast series. The remainder of liver MRI and chest, abdominal and pelvic staging shows no additional lesions. The whole appendix specimen contains a 2.6-cm well-differentiated grade-1 neuroendocrine tumor with a clear base margin; the mesoappendix was removed. {patientName} has recovered and remains fit for surgery.
after.task: Which next management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s appendiceal tumor after these acquired staging results?
after.reviewOrderNotice: key shown first for review only.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with right hemicolectomy and regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: The acquired MRI observations characterize the represented liver lesions as simple cysts rather than leaving them indeterminate for staging. In this fit patient, the whole-specimen tumor size supports regional resection despite a clear appendectomy margin.

answerChoices.label: Finish resection with appendectomy and follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The liver findings have benign cyst morphology, but the completely measured primary is larger than the guideline boundary for appendix-only treatment. A clear base does not address regional nodal risk.

answerChoices.label: Obtain liver core biopsy before further resection
answerChoices.rationale: These are resolved fluid-signal, nonenhancing lesions without internal solid tissue on adequate MRI, not persistent indeterminate targets. Biopsy would add an unsupported staging step. This conclusion comes from morphology, not a negative receptor scan.

after.explanation: The earlier CT uncertainty must be updated using the actual MRI: simple fluid signal, a thin wall and no enhancing internal tissue characterize the represented lesions as cysts. This is different from inferring cysts from absent receptor uptake. The whole-specimen primary exceeds the directly sourced greater-than-2-cm NET boundary, so regional nodal resection remains indicated despite a clear base margin. A smaller favorable tumor or unresolved liver staging would change this decision.

manualAuthorGate.interpret: Use adequate precontrast, fluid-sensitive and postcontrast MRI morphology to resolve the two actual CT targets as simple cysts rather than assuming that absent receptor activity proves benignity.
manualAuthorGate.apply: With those staging targets resolved, apply the complete primary specimen and regional nodal indication rather than treating local margin clearance as completion of all surgery.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Defer the operative plan for liver biopsy because the earlier CT used the word indeterminate, without incorporating the later morphology.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Both actual CT targets are resolved on dedicated MRI as homogeneous fluid-signal lesions without enhancing internal tissue; the complete primary measures 2.6 cm.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: An unnecessary invasive staging step delays the regional plan, or appendix-only treatment leaves the regional basin unaddressed.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Without the dedicated MRI, the prior CT uncertainty remains and immediate regional planning is underspecified. Without the full primary measurement, the regional indication is not established. The clear margin distinguishes local from regional treatment. Grade and mesoappendix information make the small-favorable counterfactual coherent.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Replace the whole-specimen primary measurement with a subcentimeter tumor lacking unfavorable features, preserving complete appendectomy with mesoappendix and benign MRI. Finish resection with appendectomy and follow-up becomes the best offered plan.
manualAuthorGate.cueAttack: The neutral task no longer repeats localized diagnosis or size. The weak cecal-cuff competitor is replaced by a staging-first plan driven by the prior actual uncertainty. All options are current post-staging management policies: finish, proceed regionally, or defer for targeted tissue. The key is neither uniquely cautious nor the only investigation with a preview.
manualAuthorGate.stageCategory: Current operative planning after acquired staging: finish treatment, proceed with regional resection, or defer for additional targeted staging.
manualAuthorGate.difficulty: Predicted moderate for PGY-2/3 from carrying an obsolete indeterminate-stage conclusion forward or confusing low grade and a negative local margin with a small favorable primary. The disputed 1-2-cm boundary is not used.
manualAuthorGate.oneBestAnswer: Adequate diagnostic cyst morphology resolves the represented staging concern; ASCRS recommendation 7 directly supports regional surgery for this greater-than-2-cm nonmetastatic primary. MRI does not claim to exclude every microscopic metastasis, and no biopsy is universally ranked against receptor imaging.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceCheck: The tracer-selection question is parked. The current version is a standalone clinic record with the earlier CT uncertainty in the header and the actual dedicated liver MRI in this update; no receptor result is invented or credited with cyst diagnosis.
manualAuthorGate.repairRecord: One response to the independent REVISE: named the modality and acquisitions, replaced the handed-down staging conclusion with supported MRI observations, neutralized the task and replaced a margin-nullified cuff with a real staging competitor. Re-solved both the smaller-primary and unresolved-liver boundaries.

distractorChecks.temptation: Equate a low grade, clear margin and benign liver findings with a small favorable NET that needs no further resection.
distractorChecks.rankingRationale: The liver findings have benign cyst morphology, but the completely measured primary is larger than the guideline boundary for appendix-only treatment. A clear base does not address regional nodal risk.
distractorChecks.counterfactual: If the fully measured tumor were smaller than 1 cm without unfavorable features and had been removed with its mesoappendix, ending resection at appendectomy would be the best offered plan.

distractorChecks.temptation: Carry the earlier CT uncertainty forward despite the newly acquired diagnostic morphology.
distractorChecks.rankingRationale: These are resolved fluid-signal, nonenhancing lesions without internal solid tissue on adequate MRI, not persistent indeterminate targets. Biopsy would add an unsupported staging step. This conclusion comes from morphology, not a negative receptor scan.
distractorChecks.counterfactual: If an enhancing solid component remained unresolved on dedicated imaging and multidisciplinary review selected tissue confirmation to determine treatment intent, liver sampling before further resection could be appropriate.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The receiving hospital's CT shows a 5.5-cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection containing gas. It abuts the bladder and rectum, with a posterior catheter path clear of bowel. No enteric contrast leak or diffuse intraperitoneal fluid is seen. Fever and focal pain persist after intravenous antibiotics. {patientName} remains alert with stable blood pressure and no diffuse rigidity.
decisionNodes.stem: Which source-control plan should be recommended now for {patientName}'s postoperative pelvic collection?

answerChoices.label: Continue intravenous antibiotics with serial examination
answerChoices.rationale: Antibiotics can suffice for selected small or resolving collections. Persistent infection with this organized accessible collection supports evacuation as part of source control.

answerChoices.label: Perform operative exploration with pelvic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Exploration can control generalized contamination, an ongoing enteric leak or a collection inaccessible to percutaneous treatment. The supplied single localized collection has a safe catheter route and stable physiology.

answerChoices.label: Perform image-guided pelvic catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent infection and an organized localized collection call for source control. The safe posterior route and absence of generalized peritonitis support image-guided catheter drainage with ongoing antimicrobial care.

decisionNodes.explanation: The organized collection and persistent fever indicate a residual source needing control. Stable physiology, localization and a safe catheter route support image-guided drainage with antimicrobial therapy. Generalized contamination or an uncontrolled enteric leak would change the source-control operation.
sourceLabels: Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis, 2020 WSES update
SAGES guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of appendicitis

WSES global intra-abdominal infection guidelines, 2017

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At later clinic review, catheter drainage has evacuated the collection, and the treating team has documented source control without ongoing bowel leakage. {patientName} has completed four days of an active antibiotic course after drainage. She is afebrile, eating, walking and free of abdominal pain. Her leukocyte count has fallen substantially and remains slightly above the laboratory reference interval. She is immunocompetent.
decisionNodes.stem: Which antibiotic plan should be recommended now for {patientName} after this completed course and source control?

answerChoices.label: Continue treatment until the leukocyte count normalizes
answerChoices.rationale: Waiting for every inflammatory laboratory value to normalize can prolong therapy after adequate source control and clinical recovery. Fixed short-course evidence supports ending the completed course in this represented patient.

answerChoices.label: End antibiotic treatment after the completed course
answerChoices.rationale: Adequate source control and complete clinical recovery support ending the completed short course. An isolated falling mildly elevated leukocyte count does not establish a need for extension.

answerChoices.label: Continue treatment pending repeat abdominal and pelvic CT
answerChoices.rationale: Clinical recovery after adequate drainage supports ending the completed course. New or persistent illness would establish a separate indication for CT assessment of residual infection while treatment is reassessed.

decisionNodes.explanation: The relevant endpoint combines adequate source control, a completed active short course and clinical recovery. The fixed-course evidence does not require normalization of every inflammatory value. A recurrence of illness would trigger reassessment of the source and treatment plan.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Review of the archived intravenous-contrast CT shows a 5.5-cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection containing gas, adjacent to the bladder and rectum. The interventional radiologist reviews the access-plane images: posterior to the collection are pelvic fat and overlying soft tissue; bowel and major vessels lie anterior or lateral to that plane. There is no diffuse intraperitoneal fluid. No enteric contrast was administered. Fever and focal pain persist during active intravenous antibiotic treatment. {patientName} remains alert with stable blood pressure and no diffuse rigidity.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment plan should be recommended now for {patientName}'s continuing postoperative illness?

answerChoices.label: Continue antibiotics with serial abdominal examination
answerChoices.rationale: Stable circulation does not establish resolution of an organized source. Persistent fever and pain with the represented collection favor evacuation while the existing antibiotics continue.

answerChoices.label: Add operative exploration with pelvic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Operation is appropriate for generalized contamination, uncontrolled leakage or anatomy that prevents effective less invasive control. The current observations demonstrate a localized target with assessed access anatomy and no generalized peritonitis. The IV-only study does not establish that a bowel leak is impossible.

answerChoices.label: Add image-guided pelvic catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent illness and an organized collection support evacuation. The radiologist-supplied geometry permits an image-guided approach while antibiotics continue. Clinical response and drainage findings must still be assessed; this is not proof that every leak has been excluded.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent fever and pain with an organized localized collection support evacuation despite stable circulation. The assessed geometry and absence of generalized peritonitis favor image-guided drainage with continued antibiotics. The CT was acquired with intravenous contrast only: no claim of a negative enteric-contrast leak study is made. An uncontrolled bowel source or clinical deterioration would require renewed assessment and may require operation.

answerChoices.label: Continue treatment until the leukocyte count normalizes

answerChoices.label: Stop antibiotic treatment

answerChoices.label: Continue treatment pending repeat abdominal and pelvic CT

manualAuthorGate.interpret: Infer an ongoing organized source from persistence during active therapy, then interpret the collection location and interventional radiologist's observed access-plane relationships.
manualAuthorGate.apply: Select image-guided evacuation with shared antibiotics for this localized accessible target, while preserving reassessment for an uncontrolled source rather than claiming that all bowel leakage was excluded.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Continue antibiotics because blood pressure is stable; the other close error is treating gas as sufficient proof that operation is required.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Persistent fever and pain accompany a single organized collection whose reviewed posterior plane contains soft tissue and fat while bowel and major vessels lie elsewhere.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Delayed evacuation of an ongoing source, or unnecessary immediate operative exploration for a target amenable to an image-guided approach.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Removing persistent illness makes continued medical care more plausible. Removing the assessed geometry makes the percutaneous route underspecified. Generalized-peritonitis observations constrain operation. The constructed 5.5-cm measurement describes this collection and does not install a universal drainage cutoff.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Replace stable circulation and absence of diffuse rigidity with deterioration and generalized involuntary rigidity. Add operative exploration with pelvic drainage becomes the best offered plan for prompt control of generalized contamination.
manualAuthorGate.cueAttack: The neutral treatment task no longer announces source control. Active antibiotics are shared background care, and every option specifies a treatment policy. The observer and anatomy are identified without calling a route safe or declaring the lesion drainable. Both procedural options carry the same existing placeholder timing profile.
manualAuthorGate.stageCategory: Current treatment of continuing postoperative illness after anatomy and antibiotic response are observed; active antibiotics continue in every option.
manualAuthorGate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard for PGY-2/3 from balancing persistent illness, stable circulation, postoperative gas and actual access anatomy. Difficulty comes from selecting a route, not from concealing safety information or inventing a leak-negative acquisition.
manualAuthorGate.oneBestAnswer: The localized target, assessed anatomy and persistent illness support image-guided drainage under the recorded WSES and Global Alliance sources. item.title: Source-control route for a localized postoperative pelvic abscess
fairness: Persistent fever and focal pain during active antibiotics plus the organized gas-containing pelvic collection support source control. Stable physiology, no generalized peritonitis and the assessed access anatomy favor image-guided drainage over continued antibiotics without drainage or immediate operative exploration.

The two steps are recognizing that persistent illness reflects a drainable localized source despite stable circulation, then choosing an appropriate route from the access geometry and distribution of illness. These are high-yield surgical source-control decisions.

The description of bowel and major vessels relative to the posterior plane is necessary procedural evidence, not a generic 'drainage is available' permission. 'Pelvic' appears in both drainage options, and the task does not name the preferred route. No meaningful wording, absolute or convergence shortcut was identified.

The IV-only CT is not claimed to exclude a bowel leak. No enteric contrast is required merely to make initial percutaneous drainage defensible in this represented stable localized scenario. The explanation appropriately preserves reassessment and possible operation for an uncontrolled source or deterioration; it does not overstate what this scan proves.

The update supplies the relevant CT result and current treatment/physiology, so this node stands alone with the presentation. After the archive-review node it also follows coherently: the newly reviewed images change the next decision. Earlier feedback teaches image adequacy, not the drainage answer.
suggestions: Retain the clinical course, access anatomy and distinction between no generalized peritonitis and proof of no leak. Do not replace those observations with an authored conclusion that the collection is 'suitable for drainage'.

clinicalCase.learningSummary: A reassuring interpretation applies to the supplied images, not to a different dataset still in the archive. Renewed fever and pain after recovery require source localization. The record establishes that complete current contrast CT images were acquired and remain available; review those images before repeating or replacing that acquisition. This conclusion depends on unchanged clinical status and adequate source images, not on the mere absence of exported files. Persistent fever and pain with an organized localized collection support evacuation despite stable circulation. The assessed geometry and absence of generalized peritonitis favor image-guided drainage with continued antibiotics. The CT was acquired with intravenous contrast only: no claim of a negative enteric-contrast leak study is made. An uncontrolled bowel source or clinical deterioration would require renewed assessment and may require operation. The relevant endpoint combines adequate source control, a completed active short course and clinical recovery. The fixed-course evidence does not require normalization of every inflammatory value. A recurrence of illness would trigger reassessment of the source and treatment plan.

manualAuthorGate.interpret: Distinguish a falling mildly elevated leukocyte count from persistent infection by using the afebrile pain-free functional recovery after documented source control.
manualAuthorGate.apply: Apply the supported short-course endpoint to the actual days received and recovery rather than declaring the course complete before asking the learner to decide.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Continue antibiotics until the leukocyte count enters the laboratory reference interval.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Documented source control and four days of active therapy with afebrile, pain-free recovery despite a mildly abnormal falling leukocyte count.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Unnecessary antimicrobial exposure and investigation.
manualAuthorGate.deletionTest: Deleting source-control adequacy or clinical recovery invalidates the stop recommendation. The mildly abnormal falling count creates the closest competing endpoint. Four days is the constructed completed course with direct support from Global Alliance statement 8, not a newly authored mandatory minimum.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Replace recovery with renewed deep pain and fever. Continuing active treatment while obtaining CT to assess a residual source becomes the best offered plan, with duration determined after reassessment.
manualAuthorGate.cueAttack: The presentation states only what was received and observed. The task does not call the course completed and the key is a plain stopping action. Laboratory normalization and repeat CT remain credible competing endpoints with rationale kept after the answer. The CT-containing choice retains exact test timing metadata.

manualAuthorGate.difficulty: Predicted moderate for PGY-2/3 from treating incomplete laboratory normalization as treatment failure despite source control and recovery.

item.title: Antibiotic endpoint despite mild residual leukocytosis

cues.why: The key is shorter than either continuation plan. This is a limited option-length cue, but a stop order naturally needs fewer words than a conditional continuation endpoint; it does not independently establish the correct answer. Do not add filler to the key merely to equalize length.

fairness: The record gives documented source control without ongoing leakage, four days of active treatment after drainage, substantial clinical recovery and immunocompetence. A slightly elevated but substantially falling leukocyte count does not by itself make continued treatment the best of these options. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the proposed stopping decision.

The two steps are interpreting the residual laboratory abnormality in the context of recovery and controlled infection, then applying a treatment endpoint rather than waiting for complete laboratory normalization. The elevated count is a credible resident trap; adequate source control is a necessary premise, not an inference that must be hidden.

Repeat CT before stopping is weaker than the leukocyte-normalization distractor because the patient is asymptomatic with documented source control, but it still represents a recognizable demand for radiographic resolution. All options address when to stop the same antibiotic course.

The explanation appropriately makes source control and recovery part of the endpoint, rather than teaching a universal fixed duration for every abdominal infection. Exact applicability remains for clinician sign-off; this review does not introduce a new duration or threshold.

The later clinic update resets the timeline clearly and supplies drainage, elapsed treatment, source-control status and current findings. It stands alone despite the historical fever in the shared presentation. The earlier drainage feedback says to continue antibiotics at the source-control stage but does not give this later stopping answer.
Antibiotic duration after adequate source control is high yield. This is moderate application of a familiar principle, not a hard item.
suggestions: Optionally tighten all three labels to similarly concise endpoint plans, without concealing the distinction between stopping now, waiting for leukocyte normalization and waiting for repeat imaging.
Keep the mild residual leukocytosis and documented recovery; removing the competing laboratory signal would turn this into uncomplicated short-course recall.

rankedConcepts.title: Persistent pain after imaging

fairness: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT is a defensible best offered request for this inflammatory acute-abdominal presentation. Haematuria creates a plausible renal-colic temptation, but delayed CT urography is a weak acute-care competitor.

suggestions: Keep the concrete CT-protocol task, but use a supported case where the urinary/inflammatory interpretation or a genuine acquisition constraint changes the protocol choice.

reviewRecords.title: Progressive focal findings after negative CT
fairness: Diagnostic laparoscopy is the defensible best offered action: the resident must reconcile a reassuring initial scan with subsequent involuntary guarding and change the management plan. Repeat imaging and continued observation represent credible overreliance on the earlier result.

The progression and guarding are necessary clinical discriminators, not a wording shortcut. Options have comparable specificity; no key-only overlap, convergence, rhetorical absolute or teaching sentence identifies the answer without clinical interpretation.
The first node is self-contained. Its explanation does not disclose the later tumor or oncologic operation.

Review scope: all 13 proposed executable nodes were reviewed, comprising one rewritten and 12 new items. Retired/replacement proposals and held/withheld records were noted but not graded. Judgments use the candidate visible fields and their sequence, not author self-assessments. This is an offline editorial review with no new source verification or clinical approval; PASS does not change needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured exam frequencies. Runtime rendering and wait previews are outside this text-only review.

reviewRecords.title: Resection after invasive appendiceal adenocarcinoma
clarityIssues: The task asks for a 'further surgical plan', but 'Complete surgical treatment with the appendectomy' means no further surgery. The intended meaning is recoverable, but the wording makes the no-operation option an awkward fit.

cues.phrase: adenocarcinoma with infiltrative glands extending into mesoappendiceal fat
cues.why: The named cancer plus the uniquely 'Oncologic' option supplies a broad cancer-to-cancer-treatment match. The diagnostic interpretation is already supplied; the added microscopic description does not create another consequential step.

cues.phrase: The appendiceal base margin is clear
cues.why: Against 'Limited cecal re-excision around the staple line', this repeats the local-clearance distinction so explicitly that the cuff option has little competitive value. Preserve the necessary margin finding, but improve the option set.

fairness: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodal assessment is the defensible offered answer for this fit patient with localized invasive disease. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
The case follows coherently from exploration to appendectomy and permanent pathology, and the update supplies enough context for standalone entry. Earlier feedback does not give away this answer.

The tested concept is important, but the displayed task mainly recalls the operation for an explicitly named invasive cancer. Staging, margin and fitness are already interpreted rather than competing evidence the resident must resolve.
suggestions: Use a neutral next-management task that accommodates both further resection and surveillance.

Build the decision around a supported specimen or staging distinction that changes the operation. Require interpretation of that distinction and then selection of extent; do not merely remove the diagnosis label while keeping an otherwise identical recall item.
Replace the already-addressed local-clearance distractor with a credible competing plan resolved by the displayed findings.

reviewRecords.title: Colonic evaluation after appendiceal abscess
clarityIssues: The initial CT leaves the organ of origin unresolved, yet the biopsy option calls the target an 'appendiceal nodule'. That option assumes a localization the presentation explicitly withholds.
The repeat CT option specifies neither a later interval nor a different acquisition. Its role is unclear when inflammatory thickening is the stated limitation.

cues.why: The final sentence names the omitted test and exactly matches the keyed procedure. A nonmedical test-taker can choose the conspicuously missing investigation.

cues.phrase: Interval abdominal and pelvic CT shows
cues.why: An apparently identical CT is offered as a distractor after the stem announces it has already been completed. The key becomes the routine unperformed test rather than the product of two consequential inferences.

fairness: Colonoscopy is a defensible next investigation for this older patient with a persistent junctional lesion. No confident clinical inaccuracy in that selection identified offline.
The explanation emphasizes synchronous disease but does not fully address the more immediate uncertainty about a cecal primary at the junction.

The explanation should not suggest that CT has exhausted its role: the record still has an obscured base, and the next case part appropriately uses later CT after inflammatory resolution. Those stages can coexist, but their timing should be explicit.
This first node stands alone and does not disclose which resection the later findings will justify.
suggestions: Give prior colonic evaluation history neutrally only as needed; avoid ending with a named missing action.
Compare credible investigations at the same current stage, including precise timing if interval imaging remains an option. Do not use an unchanged completed study as a disposable foil.
Keep the lesion's origin uncertain consistently and explain what luminal evaluation can and cannot establish before the later appendiceal assessment.

reviewRecords.title: Persistent appendiceal lesion despite normal colonoscopy
fairness: The resident must interpret normal luminal findings as insufficient to dismiss a persistent appendiceal mural lesion, then choose limited intact excision rather than surveillance or an unproven oncologic extension. Both distinctions affect the proposed care.
The later CT adds consequential localization and base-clearance information that the initial presentation lacked. This supports the extent decision rather than simply repeating an earlier conclusion.

The record supports interval appendectomy as the best offered plan in this fit older patient with persistent suspicious imaging. This is not a blanket recommendation for every patient after an abscess; the explanation appropriately limits the application.

The sequence is coherent, and the update independently supplies the colonoscopy and repeat-imaging results. Earlier feedback establishes a neoplasm workup but does not name the keyed operation. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

reviewRecords.title: Initial resection of a distended intact appendix
clarityIssues: The patient is reviewing a proposed operation after diagnostic laparoscopy, yet 'Definitive pathology is pending' appears before any tissue acquisition is described. It is unclear whether the appendix remains in situ, a biopsy was obtained, or the question retrospectively asks what should have been done.
The task tests resection extent, while much of the explanation teaches intact retrieval and rupture avoidance, which none of the option labels distinguishes.

cues.phrase: a narrow segment of normal-appearing tissue, and the appendix separates from the cecum
cues.why: The two adjacent descriptions strongly signal a limited appendix-only field against partial cecectomy and hemicolectomy. They are relevant anatomy, but the offered choices turn them into a simple smallest-resection match with little competing reasoning.

fairness: Appendectomy with intact removal is a defensible initial extent for the described separable lesion with a normal base and no evident peritoneal disease. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
This is mainly one extent-of-resection rule. The lesion's exact biology remains unknown, but that uncertainty does not create a strong alternative among the displayed operations.
The subsequent whole-specimen LAMN result is a plausible continuation once appendectomy is explicitly established. The initial chronology should be repaired before the pair is used.
suggestions: State whether this is a retrospective decision at the index laparoscopy or a prospective plan for an unresected lesion; do not describe pathology as pending without specifying the sampled tissue.
Choose whether the objective is operative extent or safe specimen retrieval and align every option with that objective.
Introduce a supported, genuinely consequential anatomic or specimen-assessment distinction that makes a close competing operation plausible, rather than adding more statements that the base is free.

reviewRecords.title: Microscopic LAMN margin after grossly complete resection
clarityIssues: 'additional-resection plan' is awkward when the intended answer is observation. Ask for the next management plan.

'Observe' leaves follow-up intensity unspecified, although the explanation properly says surveillance planning is a separate decision. Clarify that the tested choice is whether to reoperate, not whether to provide follow-up.
fairness: There is a worthwhile two-step distinction: interpret microscopic margin involvement in a noninfiltrative, nonperforated lesion with gross clearance, then decide whether further surgery is justified. The positive-margin finding provides real tension with observation.

Observation is plausible, and formal right hemicolectomy appears disproportionate to the supplied findings. However, the displayed explanation cites limited supporting data without establishing why limited cecal re-excision is not also a defensible choice for viable mucinous epithelium at the margin. Evidence against routine right colectomy does not by itself settle observation versus local re-excision.

This is an unresolved single-best-answer concern, not a confident declaration that observation is clinically incorrect. Offline review cannot independently establish the current strength or scope of the claimed guidance. Obtain Melissa's explicit judgment on the exact observation-versus-cuff comparison before acceptance.

Broad LAMN management is relevant to residents; this precise limited-evidence margin exception is a less secure commonly tested target, hence highYield=false for this exact node rather than for the disease generally.

The update is self-contained and coherently advances to permanent pathology. Earlier feedback about a cuff when the base is involved could make a learner consider re-excision; that is legitimate tension requiring a clear explanation, not answer leakage.
suggestions: Resolve the exact margin-management comparison with the named clinician and supporting evidence; keep this version needs_clinician_review and do not treat author confidence as consensus.

If local re-excision remains a reasonable alternative under the represented facts, change the scored decision or remove the item from single-best-answer use rather than inventing additional exclusions.
If retained, explicitly explain why the microscopic epithelial margin in this complete nonperforated specimen does or does not justify local re-excision, while preserving the evidence limitation.

reviewRecords.title: Referral for cellular mucinous peritoneal disease

cues.why: The named involved compartment directly matches 'Peritoneal surgery'. Together with disease spanning pelvis and upper abdomen, this lets a nonmedical reader favor the only option explicitly naming the full affected compartment.

The key offers assessment before committing to treatment; competitors commit to 'initial systemic chemotherapy' or 'completion right hemicolectomy'. The only cautious review option is structurally advantaged.

fairness: Specialist peritoneal-surface assessment is the defensible offered referral. The explanation appropriately makes cytoreduction/HIPEC contingent on specialist assessment rather than promising that every patient is a candidate.

The low-grade neoplasm, cellular implant and broad distribution already establish the relevant disease category. Selecting the named specialty is mainly recognition and referral matching, not two consequential inferences.
This standalone item supplies sufficient patient and disease context. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Compare plans at the same level of commitment: equally specific assessments or equally specific treatments, rather than one review against two immediate treatments.

Build a real management fork using supported distribution, resectability or histologic findings whose interpretation changes the plan. Do not make the intended specialty the only option that addresses the named disease compartment.
If retained as basic referral recognition, obtain explicit acceptance of that educational purpose instead of calling it difficult resident reasoning.

reviewRecords.title: Goblet cell tumor despite historical carcinoid terminology
fairness: The resident must reconcile the historical carcinoid label and focal neuroendocrine staining with infiltrative mucin-filled goblet-cell morphology, then choose the adenocarcinoma surgical pathway rather than applying a small-NET treatment rule. The 1.4-cm size creates a credible competing interpretation rather than arbitrary extra data.

Right hemicolectomy is a defensible offered plan for localized goblet cell adenocarcinoma under the guideline-based approach described. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline; exact-version clinical approval remains separate.

The cecal-cuff option is weaker because the base is clear, but appendectomy completion remains a meaningful near-miss under the historical terminology. No decisive nonmedical cue, convergence or option-length shortcut identified.
The complete pathology review, staging, colonoscopy and surgical fitness make this standalone node understandable without another case part.

reviewRecords.title: Functional staging of a well-differentiated appendiceal NET
clarityIssues: 'should next complete' suggests that the chosen functional study will necessarily resolve two small indeterminate liver lesions. The explanation more appropriately says it 'can clarify' staging.
fairness: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT is a defensible best choice among these functional studies for the stated well-differentiated NET. The tracer labels are parallel and do not reveal the answer through ordinary word matching.

The stem supplies the diagnosis and grade, while the task preselects functional imaging. The remaining decision is primarily recall of the appropriate tracer. Removing the liver findings would still leave the same preferred tracer among these options; the lesions do not earn a second consequential inference.

A neutral next-investigation task would need to account for dedicated anatomic liver characterization as a credible alternative. This review does not assert that such imaging must precede receptor imaging in this patient.

The following update says 'completed liver characterization shows simple cysts' without identifying which study did that work. It is plausible that additional imaging occurred, but the sequence should not imply that a negative receptor study by itself proves simple cysts.
suggestions: Use 'add to staging' rather than a promise to complete it, unless the returned studies genuinely establish the necessary findings.

For a difficult item, compare clinically credible next investigations using actual acquisition limitations and a supported purpose for the next study; reverify the ranking rather than simply deleting 'functional'.
Alternatively, explicitly seek acceptance as a focused tracer-selection item. In the later update identify the study or studies that established benign liver morphology.

reviewRecords.title: Regional resection for a 2.6-cm appendiceal NET
clarityIssues: The follow-up does not identify how the indeterminate liver findings became simple cysts. It is otherwise self-contained and explicitly states the completed staging conclusion.
'further surgical plan' is an awkward lead-in for the option that means no further operation.

cues.why: The task repeats exactly the diagnosis, staging conclusion and measurement needed for the size-rule answer. It highlights the discriminator rather than asking the learner to interpret the acquired findings.

This explicitly weakens 'Re-excise the appendiceal base with a cecal cuff'. The key is then distinguished from stopping largely by recalling the size boundary. Retain margin status but choose a stronger competitor.

fairness: Right hemicolectomy with regional nodes is the defensible offered guideline-based answer for the represented fit patient with a localized 2.6-cm tumor. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.

The acquired exclusion of metastases is clinically useful, but it is handed to the learner as a conclusion. Neither interpreting raw liver findings nor resolving a management tradeoff is required. This is a high-yield threshold-recall item rather than two-step reasoning.

Prior receptor-imaging feedback does not give away the resection threshold. The chronology is plausible, subject to specifying the liver characterization rather than implying receptor imaging alone established cysts.
suggestions: Use a neutral next-management task without repeating the keyed size and localized diagnosis.
Require a supported interpretation of specimen or staging evidence that changes what operation is appropriate, with a credible alternative at that same decision stage.
Do not manufacture difficulty by moving into a disputed intermediate-size category without resolving its evidence and clinician-review requirements.

reviewRecords.title: Imaging renewed symptoms after perforated appendicitis

cues.why: This contrasts directly with the narrow superficial target in 'Targeted ultrasound of the abdominal port sites'. A reader can reject that option on location alone.
The stem adds an option-specific reassuring finding at the very site named in the weak ultrasound distractor, further removing its plausibility.

cues.phrase: renal function is within its reporting interval and no prior iodinated-contrast reaction is recorded
cues.why: Only the keyed choice requests contrast. These eligibility details are legitimate safety context, but alongside two weak competitors they prominently rehearse permission for the key instead of supporting a difficult choice.

fairness: Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT is the defensible best offered investigation for renewed fever and deep pain after initial recovery from perforated appendicitis. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.

Inferring a postoperative intra-abdominal complication and choosing CT is conceptually sequential, but neither step competes meaningfully with these distractors for the target resident audience. The nominal diagnosis-then-test chain does not establish two consequential steps.
The first node is self-contained. Its explanation prepares the general source-localization context without specifying the later drainage route.
suggestions: Replace the anatomically mismatched superficial ultrasound option with an investigation a resident could reasonably consider for the actual postoperative problem.

Make acquisition adequacy, a real competing postoperative mechanism or a supported sequencing issue consequential to the test choice. Do not merely add more clinical details to a generic CT-recognition task.
Retain necessary contrast safety information while avoiding a sequence of negatives written solely to eliminate alternatives.

reviewRecords.title: Source control for a localized postoperative pelvic collection
clarityIssues: 'No enteric contrast leak' is reported without saying that enteric contrast was administered or reached the relevant bowel. The earlier imaging task names intravenous contrast only. The reader cannot tell what this negative observation establishes.

cues.why: The task already announces the treatment objective that the resident should infer. 'Continue intravenous antibiotics with serial examination' is then a conspicuous nonprocedural outlier rather than a full competitor for a neutral next-treatment decision.

cues.phrase: a posterior catheter path clear of bowel
cues.why: This prelabels the anatomic finding as a catheter route and overlaps with the keyed 'pelvic catheter drainage'. Access information is necessary; the concern is its preinterpretation and the lack of a remaining credible route tradeoff, not the presence of anatomy itself.

fairness: The resident can make two useful inferences: the persistent illness and organized gas-containing collection require evacuation, and the localized accessible collection with stable physiology favors image-guided drainage over operative exploration. The clinical construct is worthwhile.
Image-guided drainage with ongoing antimicrobial care is a defensible best offered plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy in that choice identified offline.

Absence of demonstrated contrast extravasation is not equivalent to proof that no bowel leak exists. The explanation should preserve that limitation; the current localized findings can still favor drainage without claiming an exhaustive leak exclusion.
The update coherently follows postoperative imaging and is sufficiently detailed for standalone entry. Prior feedback does not disclose the drainage route.
suggestions: Ask for the next treatment plan without naming source control in the task.
Specify the actual acquisition and relevant contrast opacification if using absence of extravasation as a discriminator, or use only the demonstrated findings without overstating leak exclusion.

Keep necessary access anatomy in neutral observed terms, identify who assessed it, and preserve meaningful competition between treatment strategies. Do not remove safety information merely to make the item harder.

reviewRecords.title: Antibiotic endpoint despite residual mild leukocytosis

cues.phrase: after this completed course and source control
cues.why: The task calls the course completed before asking whether to continue it, and the key repeats 'after the completed course'. A nonmedical reader can match completion to ending treatment without weighing the leukocyte count or clinical recovery.

fairness: Ending therapy is a defensible offered plan given documented source control, four days of active treatment and clinical recovery. The isolated improving mild leukocytosis creates a real competing reason someone might unnecessarily extend therapy.

The clinical reasoning has two consequential components: assess whether the residual laboratory abnormality indicates ongoing illness in this recovered patient, then apply an appropriate antibiotic endpoint after source control. The current wording supplies a shortcut around those components.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline. This review does not newly verify the exact duration claim; its supporting evidence and exact-version clinical approval remain required.
The later-review framing clearly supersedes the initial febrile presentation. The update is self-contained, and earlier drainage feedback does not disclose the antibiotic duration or stopping rule.
suggestions: State neutrally that the patient has received four days of active antibiotics after drainage; do not call the course completed before the decision.
Use 'Which antibiotic plan should be recommended now?' and a plain stopping option without repeating a completion conclusion.
Preserve the recovery trajectory, source-control facts and residual leukocytosis; these are the useful competing evidence. Recheck the exact text for cue removal without expanding the vignette.

independentReviewRound1.reviewScope: Independent editorial review; no clinical approval.
independentReviewRound1.instruction: Preserve PASS exactly; revise returned items once, or park unresolved fairness. Only five topic files may be written.

definitions.presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, is assessed in the acute surgical clinic after an abdominal CT reported an air-filled appendix and no acute cause of her pain. The acquisition covered the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast. During hospital observation, tenderness became more focal on the right and involuntary guarding developed. Pregnancy testing is negative and her circulation remains stable.

nodes.displayName: Progressive symptoms after negative imaging
nodes.learningObjective: Integrate adequate negative imaging with a worsening serial examination to choose further operative evaluation.
nodes.stem: Which hospital evaluation should be recommended now for {patientName}'s worsening right-sided abdominal findings?

choices.label: Repeat contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT
choices.rationale: A repeat scan can help when the original acquisition was inadequate or a new localization problem develops. Here, adequate imaging has been followed by a progressively abnormal serial examination, supporting exploration.
choices.temptation: Treat the earlier scan as an imaging problem that another identical study will settle.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete outside acquisition with an unexamined symptomatic region would favor obtaining appropriate cross-sectional imaging before exploration.

choices.label: Proceed to diagnostic abdominal laparoscopy
choices.rationale: Progressive focal pain with new involuntary guarding keeps an operative abdominal cause consequential despite the adequate negative CT. Exploration can establish and treat the cause.
